title: data-quality-frameworks Review: Useful Checklist, Broken Main File
description: We ran data-quality checks on our 26,001-skill registry with this skill. The quality dimensions gave the checks a shape and found real problems. The main file has a block of stray code in the middle, and everything assumes a data warehouse.

author.name: TrustedSkills Team
author.bio: We assess AI agent skills by installing them, running them against real work, and reading the source. We don't accept payment for reviews.

basisNote: Part of a batch of thirteen data and automation skills run on the same day against the same dataset: this site's own registry index, 26,001 skills in one 71 MB JSON file. Each run worked in its own private copy of the site's repository. One run on one dataset is one data point, not a benchmark.

runs.task: Define and run data-quality checks on the registry index for the fields the site displays: unique slugs; complete names, descriptions, categories, install commands and repo links; valid status, tier and category values against the site's own allowed values; and consistency between fields. Write the checks as a runnable script and report pass/fail counts with sample failures.
runs.outcome:
`npx skills add wshobson/agents --skill data-quality-frameworks` installed it first time.

The skill is built on Great Expectations, dbt tests and data contracts, for tables in a warehouse. Our data is one JSON file. The agent kept the skill's quality dimensions (completeness, validity, uniqueness, consistency) and wrote the checks in plain Python instead.

The main SKILL.md is damaged. After the pointer to its reference file, about 35 lines of a report generator appear with no heading and no opening code fence. The same code sits properly in the bundled reference file.

The script ran 14 checks. Slugs were all unique and names, descriptions and categories were complete. It found 234 skills with no install command, 219 with no repo link, and 178 with no tier value, which the site's own type does not allow. About 3,900 skills (15%) have an install command that names a different owner or repo from their repo link, and most of those are still marked as installing. We re-counted each of these ourselves.

An independent Node check disagreed with the script by 8 rows on the owner/repo check. The agent traced it to a regex bug in its own script and fixed it.
runs.environment: Claude Code subagent (Sonnet 5) with the installed SKILL.md loaded as its instructions, in a private clone of the TrustedSkills website repo at commit 5169470. Python standard library only; cross-checked in Node.

summary: The quality dimensions are a good way to organise checks, and on our data they led to real findings: missing install commands, missing tiers, and thousands of install commands that disagree with their repo links. But the main file has a block of broken code in the middle, and every example assumes Great Expectations or dbt on warehouse tables. Treat it as a checklist, not a framework.

strengths.title: A clear set of quality dimensions
strengths.body: Completeness, validity, uniqueness, consistency, timeliness. Each one turned into a concrete check on our data.

strengths.title: Found real problems
strengths.body: Missing install commands, a missing tier on 178 skills, and about 3,900 install commands that point at a different repo from the listing.

strengths.title: Good material in the reference file
strengths.body: Great Expectations suites, dbt tests and data contracts are covered in full, if that is your stack.

limitations.title: Damaged main file
limitations.body: About 35 lines of report-generator code sit in SKILL.md with no heading or opening fence, after the pointer to the references.

limitations.title: Assumes a warehouse
limitations.body: Every example is Great Expectations, dbt or SQL tables. For a file or an API export, you translate it yourself.

limitations.title: No advice on checking the checks
limitations.body: Our script had a regex bug that only an independent recount caught. The skill does not suggest cross-checking.

bestFor.title: Teams already on dbt or Great Expectations
bestFor.body: Read the reference file, not the damaged SKILL.md, and recount key failures with a second tool.

notFor: Quick checks on a single file. The dimensions help, but the framework setup is more than the job needs.
